name: Sable-Reliquary
geological_features: Dark basalt surface with high iron content
Collapsed lava tube ceilings creating trench formations
specific_features: Sealed underground chambers containing preserved alien artifacts
Surface markers of unknown origin indicating chamber locations
description: Sable-Reliquary is a dark, quiet world whose basalt surface absorbs more light than it reflects, giving the planet a muted, shadowy appearance from orbit. The iron-rich geology stains everything in shades of deep gray and black, the landscape a somber expanse of solidified lava flows, collapsed lava tubes, and ancient impact craters slowly filling with wind-deposited dust. The thin atmosphere supports occasional dust movement but little else, the planet's geological activity having ceased millions of years ago when its core cooled below the threshold for volcanism.

The darkness of the surface creates an environment of muted contrasts, the basalt absorbing heat during the day and radiating it slowly through the long nights. Surface markers, geometric arrangements of dark stone that are invisible from orbit but unmistakable at ground level, dot the landscape at irregular intervals. These markers were not identified as artificial until a ground survey team noticed their consistent orientation relative to the planet's magnetic poles, each marker pointing to a location directly below it where ground-penetrating radar reveals sealed underground chambers.

The chambers contain artifacts of alien origin, sealed in vacuum conditions and preserved in a state that suggests deliberate storage rather than burial. The artifacts include objects of unknown function, containers sealed with mechanisms that resist opening, and what appear to be data storage devices in formats incompatible with any known technology. The civilization that created them left no other trace on the planet or in the system, using Sable-Reliquary as a repository for objects they wished to preserve without maintaining a permanent presence. Fifty-three chambers have been identified, and twelve have been opened, each containing a unique collection of items with no apparent thematic connection.

The archaeological significance of Sable-Reliquary has made it one of the most studied worlds in the sector, with research teams from multiple institutions competing for access to unopened chambers. The artifacts already recovered have defied full analysis, their materials and construction techniques offering glimpses of technology that operates on principles not yet understood by human science. The iron and nickel deposits are commercially significant but secondary to the archaeological value, and mining operations are confined to regions far from any identified markers. The question of why this particular world was chosen as a reliquary, and whether the builders intend to return for their stored belongings, generates as much speculation as the artifacts themselves.
